cur: Numbers opens in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the second month of the second year — the Torah is suddenly precise about its chronology, as if the nation has moved from mythic time into historical time.
new: Numbers opens in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the second month of the second year after the Exodus, one month after the Tabernacle was set up (Numbers 1:1; Exodus 40:17).

cur: The results are tabulated: Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, Gad, Naphtali — 603,550 men of fighting age, not counting the Levites who are exempt from military service because they serve the Tabernacle.
new: The results are tabulated: Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, Naphtali — 603,550 men of fighting age, not counting the Levites, who are not enrolled with the other tribes because they are put in charge of the Tabernacle.

cur: Judah leads the east side, the place of honor and first march.
new: Judah leads the east side, which the Torah calls the front, and marches first (Numbers 2:3, 2:9).

cur: If taken literally, the Sinai peninsula could not have supported such a population.
new: Many scholars argue that the Sinai desert could not naturally have supported such a population.

cur: This ambivalence explains why the census in Numbers is conducted via a half-shekel coin per person rather than a direct headcount: the coins are counted rather than people themselves.
new: The Torah does not say how the census in Numbers was taken, but Ramban (on Numbers 1:3) says it was done through half-shekels, as in Exodus 30:12-13, so that the coins were counted rather than the people themselves.

cur: The command to count Israelites 'by their hosts' is read by Rashi as indicating that God loves Israel so much that God counts them constantly — but the mechanism of indirect counting (through coins or other proxies) becomes a standard principle in Jewish law.
new: Rashi on Numbers 1:1 says God counts Israel often because they are dear to Him, and the Talmud (Yoma 22b) teaches that it is forbidden to count Jews directly, so counting through proxies became the rule in Jewish law.

cur: Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Hittite records all include population counts and military rosters.
new: Records from Mari in Mesopotamia describe periodic censuses of tribes, taken for military conscription, taxation and land distribution.

cur: The tribal organization described in Numbers — with each tribe occupying a designated quadrant around a central sacred space — mirrors the layout of Egyptian military camps, which were organized with the pharaoh's tent in the center and contingents arranged by position of honor around it.
new: Some scholars, such as Michael Homan, compare the Tabernacle at the center of the camp to Egyptian military camps like that of Ramesses II at Kadesh, which had the pharaoh's tent at its center.

cur: Then a series of laws address conditions that require leaving the camp — anyone with tzara'at or a bodily discharge — maintaining the holiness of the Israelite camp as a divine dwelling.
new: Then a series of laws address conditions that require leaving the camp — anyone with tzara'at, a bodily discharge, or impurity from a corpse — maintaining the holiness of the Israelite camp as a divine dwelling.

cur: The Sotah ritual — one of the Torah's most controversial passages — addresses jealousy within marriage: a husband who suspects his wife of infidelity may bring her before the priest, who administers a water ordeal involving sacred ink dissolved in the water; if she is guilty, the water causes physical harm; if innocent, she is cleared and the Torah says she will conceive.
new: The Sotah ritual — one of the Torah's most controversial passages — addresses jealousy within marriage: a husband who suspects his wife of infidelity may bring her before the priest, who has her drink holy water mixed with dust from the Tabernacle floor and with written curses rubbed off into it; if she is guilty, the water causes physical harm; if innocent, she is cleared and the Torah says she will conceive.

cur: The Priestly Blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) is the oldest text in the Hebrew Bible for which we have physical archaeological evidence: two tiny silver scrolls discovered in 1979 at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem, dating to the late 7th century BCE (roughly 2,600 years ago), contain these exact words.
new: The Priestly Blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) appears in the oldest surviving texts known from the Hebrew Bible: two tiny silver scrolls discovered in 1979 at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem, dated to the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, carry a shorter version of the blessing.

cur: The Priestly Blessing is recited by kohanim (priestly descendants) in every synagogue service worldwide — daily in Israel, on holidays in the diaspora.
new: The Priestly Blessing is recited by kohanim (priestly descendants) in synagogue: daily in Israel and in most Sephardic communities, and only on festivals in Ashkenazi communities outside Israel.

cur: The Talmud specifies that it must be chanted with joy, not grudgingly, and that kohanim must wash their hands (duchening) before ascending to bless.
new: The Talmud (Sotah 39a) gives the kohanim a blessing to say first, ending 'to bless His people Israel with love,' and rules that a kohen who has not washed his hands may not bless.

cur: During the Amida prayer, the congregation covers their faces with their tallitot, as the blessing is considered a moment of concentrated divine presence.
new: During the repetition of the Amida, the kohanim cover their heads with their tallitot, and the congregation's custom is not to look at them.

cur: Parents bless their children with the Priestly Blessing every Friday night at the Shabbat table.
new: Many parents bless their children with the Priestly Blessing on Friday night at the Shabbat table.

cur: The Nazirite vow, though largely obsolete today, became the model for various Jewish ascetic traditions and remains a legally recognized category in halakha.
new: The Nazirite vow is rare today but remains a category in Jewish law.

cur: The Sotah water ordeal has no direct parallel in other ancient Near Eastern law, though water ordeals appear in Mesopotamian legal practice (the Code of Hammurabi prescribes an ordeal by river for certain accusations).
new: The closest ancient parallel is in the Code of Hammurabi (law 132), which says a wife suspected of adultery but not caught must undergo an ordeal by the river.

cur: Second-Temple-era texts from Qumran and later rabbinic sources show that the Sotah ritual was actually practiced during the Temple period, administered by the priests in Jerusalem, before being formally suspended by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai after the Temple's destruction.
new: The Mishnah (Sotah 9:9) says the ritual of the bitter waters stopped when adulterers became many, and that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai put an end to it.

cur: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses; Miriam is struck with tzara'at and then healed.
new: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses; Miriam is struck with tzara'at, shut out of the camp for seven days, and then brought back.

cur: She is healed after seven days of quarantine, the whole camp waiting for her.
new: She is shut out of the camp for seven days, and the people do not march on until she is brought back.

cur: When two young men, Eldad and Medad, prophesy independently in the camp rather than at the tent of meeting, Joshua urgently tells Moses to stop them.
new: When two of the elders, Eldad and Medad, prophesy in the camp rather than at the Tent of Meeting, Joshua urgently tells Moses to stop them.

cur: This verse became a touchstone for mystical and pietist movements throughout Jewish history.

The portion's account of Moses's breaking point — 'I cannot carry this people alone' — is read by the rabbis as a model of authentic human leadership: Moses does not pretend to be invulnerable, and his complaint leads God to create a collaborative governance structure (the seventy elders) rather than dismissing him.
new: When Moses says he cannot carry this people alone, God answers by having seventy elders share the burden with him (Numbers 11:17).

cur: The 'passing of spirit' from Moses to the seventy elders is seen in Jewish tradition as the origin of the Sanhedrin — the seventy-one-member supreme religious-legal council that governed Jewish life through the Second Temple period.
new: The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 1:6) learns from this passage that the Great Sanhedrin, the supreme court, had seventy-one judges: the seventy elders plus Moses.

cur: Miriam's challenge to Moses ('has God only spoken through Moses? Has he not spoken through us too?') raised a genuine theological question about prophetic hierarchy that the Torah answers but the tradition has returned to repeatedly.
new: Miriam and Aaron's challenge to Moses ('Has God spoken only through Moses—and not through us as well?') raises a question about prophetic rank that the Torah answers in the next verses.

cur: God is furious at the lack of faith and decrees that the entire generation will die in the desert over forty years — only their children will enter the land.
new: God decrees that everyone counted from age twenty and up who complained will die in the desert over forty years; only their children, with Caleb and Joshua, will enter the land.

cur: They return carrying enormous grape clusters on a pole as proof of the land's fertility, and ten of the twelve deliver a report laced with demoralization: the cities are fortified and enormous, the people are like giants ('we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and so we seemed in their eyes'), and conquest is impossible.
new: They return carrying a single cluster of grapes on a pole between two men, with pomegranates and figs, and ten of the twelve deliver a report laced with demoralization: the cities are fortified and enormous, the people are like giants ('we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and so we seemed in their eyes'), and conquest is impossible.

cur: The phrase 'we seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes — and so we seemed in their eyes' is the Torah's most devastating piece of psychological insight: the spies have no way of knowing how the Canaanites perceive them, yet they project their own self-image onto their enemies. The rabbis note that this inner defeat preceded any military failure.
new: The spies say 'we looked like grasshoppers to ourselves, and so we must have looked to them' (Numbers 13:33). The Talmud (Sotah 35a) asks how they could know what the Canaanites thought: one rabbi says they were lying, and another answer says they overheard the Canaanites calling them grasshoppers.

cur: The day the spies returned with their bad report — the ninth of Av (Tisha B'Av) — became the most catastrophic date in Jewish history: the first Temple was destroyed on that date, the second Temple was destroyed on that date, and numerous other disasters are associated with it in tradition.
new: According to the Talmud (Taanit 29a), the night the people wept over the spies' report was the ninth of Av (Tisha B'Av), and the Mishnah (Taanit 4:6) lists other disasters on that date, including the destruction of the First and Second Temples.

cur: The Talmud (Sotah 35a) derives from this story the principle that lashon hara (evil speech) about the land of Israel is as serious as evil speech about people.
new: The Talmud (Arakhin 15a) reasons from this story that if the spies were punished so severely for speaking badly about the wood and stones of the land of Israel, someone who speaks badly about another person will be punished even more.

cur: Tisha B'Av, the fast day commemorating both Temple destructions, is rooted in this night when Israel wept without cause and was told by God: 'I will give you cause to weep in all future generations.'
new: The Talmud (Sotah 35a; Taanit 29a) links Tisha B'Av, the fast day commemorating both Temple destructions, to this night, teaching that because Israel wept without cause, God set the day as a day of weeping for future generations.

cur: The Late Bronze Age Canaan the spies were sent to scout was genuinely fortified and urbanized. Cities like Hazor (the largest city in Canaan at its peak) had massive rampart walls and palace complexes; Megiddo, Lachish, and Gezer were similarly imposing. Egyptian Execration Texts and the Amarna Letters confirm the political complexity and military strength of Canaanite city-states. The 'giants' (Nephilim) mentioned by the spies may reflect the Israelites' encounter with chariot-owning professional armies — a technology they had never faced — translated into the language of superhuman beings.
new: The Torah does not tie the spies' mission to an archaeological period. Hazor was the largest city in Canaan in the Late Bronze Age, when Egypt ruled the region, and the Amarna Letters, written by Canaanite rulers to Egypt in the 1300s BCE, show many small city-states, some of whose rulers pleaded with Egypt for troops.

cur: The next day the community blames Moses and a plague begins, killed only when Aaron runs into the crowd with incense to atone.
new: The next day the community blames Moses and Aaron and a plague begins, stopped only when Aaron runs into the crowd with incense to atone.

cur: The confrontation at the Tabernacle entrance ends with God telling Moses and Aaron to separate from the congregation so divine fury can consume them; Moses successfully intercedes again; but then the earth opens below Korach, Datan, Abiram, and their households — they go down alive into the pit with all their possessions — and fire from God consumes the 250 men offering incense.
new: The confrontation at the Tabernacle entrance ends with God telling Moses and Aaron to separate from the congregation so divine fury can consume them; Moses and Aaron successfully plead again; but then the earth opens below Korach, Datan, Abiram, and their households (though Korach's sons did not die, Numbers 26:11) — they go down alive into the pit with all their possessions — and fire from God consumes the 250 men offering incense.

cur: Korach's argument — 'the entire community is holy, every one of them' — is a direct quote from Leviticus 19:2 ('you shall be holy'), making it a case where scripture is used to argue against the very authority that transmitted scripture.
new: Korach's argument, 'all the community are holy, all of them' (Numbers 16:3), uses the same word for 'holy' as God's command in Leviticus 19:2, 'You shall be holy.'

cur: In the Talmud (Avot 5:17), Korach's name became shorthand for illegitimate power grabs dressed up in the language of justice.

The rebellion of Korach has been interpreted throughout Jewish history as the paradigmatic warning against populist challenges to legitimate religious authority — and equally as a caution against abuse of authority that invites such challenges. Medieval biblical commentators noted that Korach's argument about universal holiness was not wrong in principle but was wrong in timing and motivation: the ideal of a 'kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6) is the goal, but the path to it requires gradual sanctification, not the abolition of all distinctions.
new: Jewish tradition reads the rebellion of Korach as a warning against challenges to legitimate authority driven by personal ambition: Rashi on 16:1 says Korach was protesting the priesthood Moses had given to his brother Aaron.

cur: The phrase 'standing between the living and the dead' — Aaron with his incense stopping the plague — became a paradigm for priestly intercession and is referenced in later Jewish martyrology.
new: The image of Aaron with his incense, standing 'between the dead and the living until the plague was checked' (Numbers 17:13), shows a priest's atonement protecting the people.

cur: The rebellion of Korach, Datan, and Abiram draws on a political reality attested throughout the ancient Near East: the tension between hereditary priestly elites and broader social groups who resented monopolized access to the divine.

The narrative's resolution — miraculous earth-swallowing, fire from heaven, and a blooming staff — uses spectacular divine intervention to settle what was fundamentally a political conflict over religious authority.
new: The Torah settles the dispute through divine signs: the earth swallowing the rebels, fire from God consuming the 250 men, and Aaron's staff sprouting to show whom God had chosen.

cur: The people erupt at Moses and Aaron ('why did you bring us out of Egypt to die?'), and God tells Moses to speak to a rock to bring water — but Moses, at the end of his endurance, strikes it twice instead and berates the people: 'Shall we bring you water from this rock?'
new: The people erupt at Moses and Aaron ('Why did you make us leave Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?'), and God tells Moses to speak to a rock to bring water, but Moses berates the people, 'Listen, you rebels, shall we get water for you out of this rock?', and strikes the rock twice.

cur: The rabbis offered dozens of explanations: he spoke angrily to the people, he gave himself and Aaron credit ('shall WE bring you water?'), he struck the rock twice suggesting doubt.
new: Commentators offered many explanations (the Or HaChaim lists ten): he spoke angrily to the people, he spoke as if he and Aaron were producing the water ('shall we get water for you?'), or he struck the rock a second time.

cur: The bronze serpent Moses made (Nechushtan) was kept by Israel and eventually became an object of illicit worship, requiring King Hezekiah to destroy it six centuries later (2 Kings 18:4).
new: The bronze serpent Moses made survived for centuries: 2 Kings 18:4 says King Hezekiah broke it into pieces because the Israelites had been offering sacrifices to it, and that it was called Nehushtan.

cur: The Talmud (Yoma 67b) states that the nations will mock Israel for this commandment, and God's response is essentially: obey it anyway.
new: Rashi on Numbers 19:2 says that Satan and the nations taunt Israel over this commandment, and that the Torah calls it a chok to say: it is a decree from God, and you have no right to question it.

cur: Both kingdoms are located in modern Jordan; Og of Bashan became legendary for his size ('his iron bed was nine cubits long' — Deuteronomy 3:11).
new: Sihon's kingdom lay in what is now Jordan, and Bashan spanned parts of modern Syria and Jordan, including the Golan Heights; Og of Bashan became legendary for his size ('his iron bed was nine cubits long' — Deuteronomy 3:11).

cur: The route of march through Edom, Moab, and Ammon tracks through the Transjordanian plateau, a real geographical corridor known from Egyptian records and archaeology.
new: Edom refused to let Israel use the King's Highway through its land, so Israel went around Edom (Numbers 20:17-21; 21:4), and its conquest of Sihon's land stopped at the border of Ammon (Numbers 21:24).

cur: The rabbis categorized Korach's dispute as the paradigmatic 'dispute not for the sake of heaven' — one motivated by personal ambition rather than truth-seeking — in contrast
new: The Mishnah (Avot 5:17) names Korach's dispute as the model of a 'dispute not for the sake of heaven', in contrast
